disp-quote.p: Overall, the manuscript has improved substantially and is now considerably clearer.
The following comments refer to the numbering of my previous review comments:
(2) If C_m is a unit vector with components h and v, these components are necessarily interdependent and therefore should not be treated or presented as independent variables.

body.p: We agree that these components are interdependent. We have corrected and clarified the description of the implemented parameter constraints. In Experiment 1, the fitted movement coefficient vector is normalised jointly with the pain coefficient, such that |C_p|+sqrt(h^2+v^2)=1; describing C_m itself as a unit vector in this experiment was therefore inaccurate. This constraint fixes an otherwise arbitrary common scale: multiplying C_p and C_m by the same positive constant leaves the predicted choices unchanged. We have corrected the definition and distinguished the searched parameters from the derived coefficient C_p in the Experiment 1 model-properties table.

Experiment 2 uses a different parameterisation: C_m is a non-negative unit vector, with h fitted and v=sqrt(1-h^2) derived. The separate vigour coefficient C_v scales the movement cost, and unit length removes the redundant scale between C_m and C_v. The average reward parameter 𝑅̅ is fixed at 1 during fitting to set the overall value scale, with C_p and C_v fitted separately. We have made these constraints explicit in the Experiment 2 model properties table and corrected its list of fitted parameters so that h and v are not presented as separately fitted parameters.
We apologise for the inaccurate description in the previous version of the manuscript and thank the reviewer for helping us identify and correct this issue.

Regarding possible concerns on statistical results involving these interdependent variables: The comparison in panel D of the Experiment 1 behaviour and modelling figure uses a two-sided paired t-test, equivalent to a one-sample test of each participant's difference h-v against zero. It does not require independence between the two components within a participant: the independent units are the participant-level differences. Following the eye-tracking exclusions described below, 20 participants contribute one difference each, giving 20-1=19 degrees of freedom. The within-participant normalisation constraint does not require a further reduction in these degrees of freedom.

We have revised the panel D caption to identify the paired test and the contrast h-v explicitly. After the eye-tracking exclusions, the updated result is t(19)=6.37, p<.001, compared with t(23)=6.72, p<.001 in the reviewed version. The qualitative conclusion remains: the fitted penalty is greater for vertical than horizontal movement.

disp-quote.p: (5) It is still not full clear to me, what the SCR analysis adds. The central argument appears to be that the relationship between decision values, pain ratings, and SCRs varies across contexts (e.g., target fixation versus painful stimulation), and that SCRs therefore capture distinct aspects of the pain experience. However, this interpretation seems to assume that SCRs measured in different contexts are established markers of separable dimensions of pain experience, which I do not find sufficiently justified.

body.p: We have revised the manuscript to distinguish the motivation for the SCR analysis, what the present evidence establishes, and the direction it motivates for further investigation. Our original question remains: what does a pain decision value estimated from choices capture about pain, and how does it relate to subjective ratings? Their correlation does not resolve whether they reflect the same aspects of pain's aversiveness or whether choice-derived values provide additional information. We introduced SCRs as a complementary physiological measurement through which to investigate this question. This rationale is now stated explicitly at the beginning of the revised SCR Results subsection, “Skin conductance responses and the interpretation of pain decision values”.

The two event contexts were chosen because of their roles in the task. Fixation on pain-associated fruit can accompany evaluation of an anticipated cost, whereas shock delivery accompanies receiving the painful stimulus. Comparing physiological associations at these stages offers a way to investigate the relationship between prospective valuation and subsequent pain experience. We agree that event timing alone does not establish either SCR response as a selective marker of a separate dimension of pain. Establishing whether these physiological responses can distinguish aspects captured by ratings and decision values is an empirical objective of this line of research.

The revised analyses do not resolve that distinction. The shock–rating association was the only association consistently supported across both experiments by the primary analysis and both sensitivity specifications. Associations involving decision values provided a less consistent pattern. We have therefore removed the double-dissociation interpretation that was added in the previous version and clarified that separate significance tests do not demonstrate differences between associations; inconclusive findings likewise do not establish equivalence between ratings and decision values. The accompanying timing, eye-tracking and SCR-estimation changes are described under Additional Changes below.

These findings refine the next question without removing the original motivation. The revised Discussion advocates combining subjective reports, choice-based models and physiological measurements to quantify where these measures converge and where they may capture distinct aspects of pain's aversiveness. In our view, future work should directly test differences between their associations and establish the functional interpretation of the physiological responses. We have revised the Results, Methods, figure caption and Discussion to make this progression from rationale, through current evidence, to future investigation explicit.

disp-quote.p: (8) I think the manuscript should state more explicitly that the assumption that "motivational vigour in a free-operant task can be quantified through an RL framework" is, in fact, a modelling assumption. While this is an interesting and promising approach, the interpretation of the model parameters depends critically on the validity and adequacy of the underlying model.

body.p: We agree that the modelling assumption should be explicit. Our aim is to provide a quantitative operationalisation of motivational vigour within a framework relating choices to movement costs and the opportunity cost of time. Movement speed and collection rate describe the behavioural expression of effort and pace, whereas C_v quantifies the weighting of vigour-related movement costs in the choice model. The model gives this quantity a precise mathematical role; interpreting it in motivational terms depends on the validity and adequacy of the framework for the task. We have revised the Discussion to explain this rationale and make that dependence explicit.

The Discussion now states: “We use motivational vigour here for the regulation of effort and pace in goal-directed behaviour, informed by accounts of competing motivations in pain (Fields, 2006). Movement speed and collection rate describe its behavioural expression, while the fitted C_v provides a choice-based operationalisation of vigour-related movement costs. Its motivational interpretation is a modelling assumption that depends on the validity and adequacy of the model; neither approach uniquely identifies motivation.”

We have also examined how well the observed choices constrain this operationalisation. The new fit profiles show that different parameter combinations attain the same minimum prediction error. Within the searched grid, equally optimal fits permit mean tonic-minus-no-tonic C_v contrasts from −4.48 to +31.74, showing that the fitted contrast, including its direction, depends on selection among optima. These are sensitivity bounds, not confidence limits. We retain the first encountered joint minimum as a reproducible reporting convention with a heuristic rationale that C_v estimated from choice trade-off is often bounded below rather than above in this foraging paradigm, and explicitly disclose its limitations in the Results.

This analysis motivates further work on both the estimation of model-based vigour and its relationship to behavioural measures. The revised Discussion proposes richer choice sets to constrain individual C_v estimates more closely, while recognising the additional search, memory and planning demands such tasks may introduce. The objective is to strengthen quantitative tests of how pain regulates effort and pace, and to establish how different operationalisations contribute to that understanding.
Additional changes made to the manuscript
Eye tracking data issue

We identified an acquisition failure in which an asynchronous eye-tracking callback stopped updating, while Unity continued ray casting with stale gaze data marked as valid. Four participants per experiment were excluded from eye-dependent analyses when an identical gaze-direction vector occurred in more than 100 frames (not necessarily consecutive) within any analysed 60-s block, leaving 20 and 27 participants, respectively, before any further analysis-specific quality exclusions. Independent Experiment 2 analyses of ratings, choice probability, whole-block hand speed and collection rate retain 31 participants; the fixation-selected reaching-trajectory analysis uses 27. The main manuscript now declares the eye-tracking exclusions. The new supplementary section, “Eye tracking methods and generation attempt”, details acquisition and quality control, exploratory HAGI gaze generation, and replay limitations. Generated data were not used to reinstate excluded participants.
SCR and EEG clock synchronisation

We added affine clock corrections to improve the alignment of SCR and EEG recordings with task events. The Methods now refer readers to the new supplementary section, “Clock synchronisation”, for the procedures, diagnostic figures and limitations.
SCR estimation and sensitivity analyses

Alongside the clock-synchronisation corrections and eye-tracking exclusions, we revised the SCR analyses to retain eligible block-level coefficients irrespective of their first-level statistical significance. A nonsignificant coefficient remains an uncertain estimate; selecting coefficients according to their significance can distort subsequent association analyses. The primary analysis therefore includes these estimates without significance-based selection. Supplementary inverse-variance models using metafor and brms incorporate differences in coefficient-estimation precision using heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) sampling variances, while allowing participant variation and additional block-level heterogeneity. These analyses assess whether the conclusions depend on how estimation uncertainty is handled. The specifications and results for both experiments are reported in the new supplementary section, “Skin conductance sensitivity analyses”.
Uncorrelated random effects model

We have clarified in the Methods (“Statistical Analysis”) that, when singular fits occurred within an analysis block, we used a no-correlation structure for the entire block of analysis, including otherwise nonsingular fits, while retaining all subject-level intercepts and random slopes included in the original specification. This applies to SCR models, EEG channel-wise fits and permutation batches. The supplementary “Linear mixed model outputs” section now includes “Maximal and no-correlation fits”, comparing the choice-distance and SCR analyses on identical observations and reporting slopes, confidence intervals, test statistics and singularity classifications for both specifications.
Cluster permutation tests

We added cluster-based permutation tests to the main manuscript alongside the existing electrode-wise Bonferroni correction and updated the channel-wise EEG results following the analysis revisions. The tonic-pain alpha cluster survives cluster correction (p=.006), although none of its individual electrodes survives Bonferroni correction. The beta association does not survive cluster correction. For fitted vigour constants, the alpha association at Pz survives Bonferroni correction (p=.042) but does not reach the cluster-corrected threshold (p=.059). The Results and Discussion now distinguish these outcomes and present the neural associations cautiously, without treating them as uniquely identifying a motivational mechanism.
Event-related and induced responses to phasic pain

In the previous version, the analysis labelled as induced oscillatory responses calculated total event-related power without subtracting the evoked response. We have revised the supplementary section to present both total-power results and induced-power estimates obtained by subtracting each participant’s condition-specific ERP before time–frequency analysis. The induced high–low phasic pain contrast was significant without tonic pain (cluster p = .0001) but not with tonic pain (smallest cluster p = .1925). Direct comparisons between tonic conditions were nonsignificant. We additionally tested the tonic-by-phasic intensity interaction on the baseline-normalised log-power scale; no significant clusters were identified for either total power (smallest cluster-level p = .8382) or induced power (smallest cluster-level p = .1575).

Interpretation is limited by unequal and sometimes sparse high-pain trial counts (3–49; mean 15.48, sample SD 10.06 across 62 participant-by-tonic-condition counts from 31 participants). The free-operant design allowed participants to avoid high-pain outcomes, and ERP estimates based on few trials may retain non-phase-locked activity and noise, limiting the separation of evoked and induced activity. We have added the following paragraph to the main-text Discussion:

“It is worth noting that, while we found no clear behavioural or ERP evidence that tonic pain modulated phasic pain responses, this does not establish that phasic pain processing is independent of tonic pain. Supplementary analyses identified a significant high-low phasic pain contrast in induced power without tonic pain but not with tonic pain; however, direct interaction tests were non-significant for both total event-related and induced power. These findings warrant caution because the free-operant task allowed participants to avoid high-pain outcomes, leaving limited and unequal high-pain trial counts. The subtracted ERP estimate may therefore retain non-phase-locked activity and noise, limiting the separation of evoked and induced activity.”
